name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Sequence of steps in Gabriel phthalimide synthesis

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following operational stages in the correct chronological sequence for the laboratory preparation of ethanamine via the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis:

I. Deprotonation of phthalimide using ethanolic potassium hydroxide to produce potassium phthalimide.
II. Nucleophilic substitution reaction of potassium phthalimide with ethyl bromide to yield N-ethylphthalimide.
III. Alkaline hydrolysis of N-ethylphthalimide using aqueous sodium hydroxide to release ethanamine and sodium phthalate.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Chemical Transformation
The objective is to synthesize ethanamine (a primary aliphatic amine) from phthalimide and ethyl bromide using the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis method.

Step 2: Relevant Principles of Gabriel Phthalimide Synthesis
Phthalimide contains an acidic hydrogen attached to nitrogen because the conjugate phthalimide anion is stabilized by resonance delocalisation across two adjacent carbonyl groups. The reaction proceeds in three distinct operational phases: generation of a strong nitrogen nucleophile, nucleophilic substitution on an aliphatic halide, and subsequent alkaline cleavage of the imide linkages.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Analysis
In the initial stage, phthalimide is reacted with ethanolic potassium hydroxide to remove the imide proton, yielding the nucleophilic potassium phthalimide salt (Stage I). Next, potassium phthalimide undergoes an \(S_N2\) nucleophilic substitution reaction upon heating with ethyl bromide, displacing bromide ion to form N-ethylphthalimide (Stage II). Finally, alkaline hydrolysis of N-ethylphthalimide with aqueous sodium hydroxide cleaves the two carbon-nitrogen single bonds of the imide ring, producing sodium phthalate and freeing the primary aliphatic amine, ethanamine (Stage III).

Step 4: Chronological Sequence Assembly
Connecting these sequential chemical transformations gives the operational order: Stage I (potassium salt formation) followed by Stage II (alkylation to N-ethylphthalimide), followed by Stage III (alkaline hydrolysis to release ethanamine). Thus, the correct chronological sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Alkylation cannot precede deprotonation because neutral phthalimide is a poor nucleophile, and hydrolysis cannot occur before alkylation because that would merely destroy the phthalimide ring before the ethyl moiety is incorporated. Hence, the unique valid sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Chronological stages of Hoffmann bromamide degradation

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following mechanistic stages in the correct chronological sequence during the conversion of propanamide to ethanamine via the Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction:

I. Formation of N-bromopropanamide by base-promoted reaction of propanamide with bromine.
II. Base-induced deprotonation of N-bromopropanamide to generate a reactive bromoamide anion.
III. Concerted migration of the ethyl group from the carbonyl carbon to nitrogen with departure of bromide ion to form ethyl isocyanate.
IV. Alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl isocyanate followed by decarboxylation to produce ethanamine and carbonate ion.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Chemical Transformation
The reaction is the conversion of an aliphatic primary amide (propanamide) into a primary amine with one fewer carbon atom (ethanamine) using bromine and aqueous or ethanolic sodium hydroxide.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Mechanistic Pathway
The Hoffmann bromamide degradation involves electrophilic bromination of nitrogen, base deprotonation to yield an electron-rich nitrogen intermediate, intramolecular 1,2-rearrangement of the alkyl group to nitrogen with concomitant loss of leaving group (bromide), and finally aqueous alkaline hydrolysis of the resulting isocyanate intermediate.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Analysis
First, propanamide reacts with bromine in the presence of base to form N-bromopropanamide (Stage I). Second, hydroxide ion abstracts the acidic proton remaining on the nitrogen of N-bromopropanamide, generating a transient bromoamide anion (Stage II). Third, the ethyl group migrates with its electron pair from the carbonyl carbon to the electron-deficient nitrogen atom while bromide ion leaves simultaneously, forming the ethyl isocyanate intermediate, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{N}=\text{C}=\text{O}\) (Stage III). Fourth, nucleophilic attack of hydroxide ion on ethyl isocyanate leads to hydrolysis and decarboxylation, releasing ethanamine, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\), and carbonate ion (Stage IV).

Step 4: Chronological Sequence Assembly
The mechanistic order proceeds without inversion: Stage I (bromination) \(\rightarrow\) Stage II (anion formation) \(\rightarrow\) Stage III (rearrangement to isocyanate) \(\rightarrow\) Stage IV (hydrolysis to primary amine). Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Rearrangement cannot occur prior to bromination and anion generation because bromide serves as the leaving group that drives the 1,2-alkyl migration. Hydrolysis occurs only on the formed isocyanate. Hence, the final correct order is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Synthetic sequence for controlled monobromination of aniline

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following synthetic steps in the correct chronological sequence for the preparation of 4-bromoaniline from aniline:

I. Protection of the amino group by treating aniline with acetic anhydride in pyridine to form acetanilide.
II. Electrophilic aromatic substitution of acetanilide using bromine in glacial acetic acid to obtain 4-bromoacetanilide.
III. Hydrolysis of 4-bromoacetanilide with dilute aqueous acid or alkali to deprotect and regenerate the primary amino group.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Synthetic Target
Target molecule: 4-bromoaniline (a monobrominated aromatic amine). Starting material: aniline.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Reactivity Considerations
The unshared electron pair of the amino group in aniline strongly activates the benzene ring via resonance (+R effect). Direct bromination with bromine water results in uncontrollable, polysubstituted 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. To obtain a monobromo derivative selectively at the para-position, the activating power of the amino group must be moderated by protection as an amide (acetamido group), followed by bromination and subsequent deprotection.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Analysis
In Stage I, aniline is treated with acetic anhydride in the presence of pyridine base. Acetylation converts the \(-\text{NH}_2\) group into an acetamido group (\(-\text{NHCOCH}_3\)), forming acetanilide. In acetanilide, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the adjacent carbonyl group, decreasing electron donation to the benzene ring and preventing polysubstitution. In Stage II, acetanilide undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with bromine dissolved in glacial acetic acid. The bulky acetamido group directs the incoming electrophile predominantly to the less sterically hindered para-position, yielding 4-bromoacetanilide. In Stage III, 4-bromoacetanilide is subjected to acidic or alkaline hydrolysis, which selectively cleaves the amide bond to regenerate the free primary amino group, producing 4-bromoaniline.

Step 4: Chronological Sequence Assembly
The proper synthetic strategy follows the order: Stage I (protection by acetylation) \(\rightarrow\) Stage II (monobromination) \(\rightarrow\) Stage III (deprotection by hydrolysis). Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Attempting bromination before protection yields 2,4,6-tribromoaniline rather than a monobromo derivative. Hydrolysis must be the terminal step to restore the amine. Hence, the correct sequential pathway is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Synthetic sequence for controlled mononitration of aniline

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following stages in the correct chronological sequence for the preparation of 4-nitroaniline as the major product starting from aniline:

I. Acetylation of aniline with acetic anhydride in pyridine to protect the activated amino group as acetanilide.
II. Electrophilic nitration of acetanilide with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid at 288 K.
III. Acid-catalysed or base-catalysed hydrolysis of the resulting 4-nitroacetanilide to afford 4-nitroaniline.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Synthetic Target
The goal is the selective synthesis of 4-nitroaniline (para-nitroaniline) from aniline without extensive oxidation or significant formation of meta-nitroaniline.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Problem with Direct Nitration
Direct nitration of aniline with concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids leads to significant oxidation of the sensitive benzene ring and extensive protonation of the amino group to the meta-directing anilinium ion (\(-\text{NH}_3^+\)), producing an undesirable mixture containing 47% meta-nitroaniline and tarry oxidation products. To prepare the 4-nitro isomer cleanly and as the predominant product, the amino group must first be protected by acetylation.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Analysis
Stage I involves reacting aniline with acetic anhydride in the presence of pyridine to produce acetanilide. The resonance interaction of the nitrogen electron pair with the carbonyl group reduces both the oxidisability and basicity of the nitrogen atom. Stage II involves treating acetanilide with a nitrating mixture (concentrated \(\text{HNO}_3\) and concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)) at 288 K. The moderately activating, sterically demanding acetamido group directs the nitronium ion (\(\text{NO}_2^+\)) predominantly to the para-position, producing 4-nitroacetanilide as the major product. Stage III involves the deprotection of 4-nitroacetanilide via acid-catalysed or base-catalysed hydrolysis, cleanly unmasking the amino group to give 4-nitroaniline.

Step 4: Chronological Sequence Assembly
The required synthetic order is Stage I (acetylation/protection) \(\rightarrow\) Stage II (nitration of acetanilide) \(\rightarrow\) Stage III (hydrolytic deprotection to yield 4-nitroaniline). Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Protecting the amino group must be carried out first to block anilinium ion formation and ring oxidation, while hydrolysis must be carried out last to recover the primary amine. Hence, the logical sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_SEQUENCING_Q05 - Sequential synthesis of orange dye from nitrobenzene

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following sequential reaction steps in the correct chronological order for the preparation of the orange azo dye, 4-hydroxyazobenzene, starting from nitrobenzene:

I. Reduction of nitrobenzene using iron scrap and hydrochloric acid to yield aniline.
II. Diazotisation of aniline with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at 273–278 K to produce benzenediazonium chloride.
III. Azo coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol in a mildly alkaline aqueous medium at pH 9–10.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Chemical Transformations
Starting material: nitrobenzene (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2\)). Target product: 4-hydroxyazobenzene (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{N}=\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{OH}\)), an orange azo dye.

Step 2: Relevant Principles of Azo Dye Synthesis
Azo dyes are formed through electrophilic aromatic substitution known as azo coupling, where a diazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile attacking an activated aromatic substrate (such as phenol). Because nitrobenzene lacks a diazonium functionality, it must first be reduced to a primary aromatic amine, converted to a diazonium salt, and then coupled.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Analysis
In Stage I, nitrobenzene is reduced using scrap iron and hydrochloric acid (\(\text{Fe} / \text{HCl}\)) to generate aniline. This is the preferred industrial method because the \(\text{FeCl}_2\) formed hydrolyses to release \(\text{HCl}\), requiring only a catalytic amount of acid. In Stage II, aniline is diazotised by treatment with nitrous acid generated in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at ice-cold temperatures (273–278 K), yielding benzenediazonium chloride (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-\)). In Stage III, benzenediazonium chloride is reacted with phenol under mildly basic conditions (pH 9–10). Base deprotonates phenol to form the strongly activated phenoxide ion, which couples at the para-position with the diazonium cation to produce 4-hydroxyazobenzene.

Step 4: Chronological Sequence Assembly
The logical chemical progression requires: Stage I (reduction of nitrobenzene to aniline) \(\rightarrow\) Stage II (diazotisation of aniline to benzenediazonium chloride) \(\rightarrow\) Stage III (alkaline azo coupling with phenol). Thus, the correct chronological sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Diazotisation requires a primary aromatic amine, so reduction must occur first. Coupling requires the diazonium electrophile, so it must occur last. Therefore, the sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Conversion sequence of aniline to fluorobenzene

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the correct chronological sequence for the synthetic conversion of aniline to fluorobenzene via the Balz–Schiemann reaction:

I. Diazotisation of aniline using sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at 273–278 K to form benzenediazonium chloride.
II. Precipitation and isolation of water-insoluble benzenediazonium fluoroborate by treating benzenediazonium chloride with fluoroboric acid.
III. Controlled thermal decomposition of dry benzenediazonium fluoroborate to yield fluorobenzene, boron trifluoride, and nitrogen gas.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Chemical Transformations
Starting material: aniline (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\)). Target product: fluorobenzene (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{F}\)).

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Balz–Schiemann Reaction
Direct fluorination of benzene with elemental fluorine is extremely violent, uncontrollable, and leads to ring destruction. The Balz–Schiemann reaction provides a safe, reproducible route to aryl fluorides by thermal cleavage of isolated aryldiazonium fluoroborate salts.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Analysis
In Stage I, aniline is converted into benzenediazonium chloride (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-\)) by treatment with sodium nitrite and excess hydrochloric acid at ice-cold temperature (273–278 K). In Stage II, aqueous fluoroboric acid (\(\text{HBF}_4\)) is added to the cold diazonium solution. Benzenediazonium fluoroborate (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{BF}_4^-\)) precipitates out as a stable, water-insoluble crystalline solid, which is filtered and dried. In Stage III, dry benzenediazonium fluoroborate is subjected to gentle, controlled heating. Pyrolysis causes expulsion of nitrogen gas and boron trifluoride, yielding pure fluorobenzene: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{BF}_4^- \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{F} + \text{BF}_3 + \text{N}_2\).

Step 4: Chronological Sequence Assembly
The order of operations is Stage I (diazotisation) \(\rightarrow\) Stage II (fluoroborate salt precipitation) \(\rightarrow\) Stage III (pyrolytic decomposition). Hence, the correct chronological sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Precipitation of the fluoroborate salt cannot occur without prior generation of the diazonium cation, and thermolysis is applied to the isolated dry salt. Thus, the only correct sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_SEQUENCING_Q07 - Synthesis of symmetrical tribromobenzene from nitrobenzene

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following chemical stages in the correct chronological sequence for the multistep synthesis of 1,3,5-tribromobenzene starting from nitrobenzene:

I. Reduction of nitrobenzene with iron scrap and hydrochloric acid to obtain aniline.
II. Electrophilic aromatic bromination of aniline using bromine water to produce 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.
III. Diazotisation of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at 273–278 K to form 2,4,6-tribromobenzenediazonium chloride.
IV. Reductive deamination of 2,4,6-tribromobenzenediazonium chloride using hypophosphorous acid and water to yield 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Synthetic Target
Starting material: nitrobenzene. Target molecule: 1,3,5-tribromobenzene (symmetrical tribromobenzene). Notice that all three bromine atoms are in meta-relationships to each other, a substitution pattern that cannot be obtained by direct bromination of benzene.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Synthetic Strategy
The amino group acts as a powerful ortho/para-directing activator that forces three bromine substituents into the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to nitrogen. Once these bromines are situated at positions 2, 4, and 6, removal of the amino group leaves bromines at positions 1, 3, and 5 of the parent benzene ring. The amino group is removed via diazotisation followed by reduction with hypophosphorous acid (\(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2\)).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Analysis
In Stage I, nitrobenzene is reduced using \(\text{Fe} / \text{HCl}\) to generate aniline. In Stage II, aniline is treated with bromine water (aqueous \(\text{Br}_2\)). Due to powerful activation by the unshared electron pair on nitrogen, bromination occurs simultaneously at both ortho-positions and the para-position to precipitate 2,4,6-tribromoaniline as a white solid. In Stage III, 2,4,6-tribromoaniline is diazotised by treatment with \(\text{NaNO}_2\) and \(\text{HCl}\) at 273–278 K, replacing the \(-\text{NH}_2\) group with the diazonium group (\(-\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-\)) to produce 2,4,6-tribromobenzenediazonium chloride. In Stage IV, the diazonium salt is treated with hypophosphorous acid (\(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2\)) and water in the presence of cuprous ions. The diazonium group is reductively replaced by hydrogen (deamination), producing 1,3,5-tribromobenzene along with nitrogen, phosphorous acid (\(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3\)), and \(\text{HCl}\).

Step 4: Chronological Sequence Assembly
The sequence must follow the order: Stage I (reduction of nitro to amine) \(\rightarrow\) Stage II (exhaustive bromination) \(\rightarrow\) Stage III (diazotisation of the tribromo intermediate) \(\rightarrow\) Stage IV (reductive deamination to 1,3,5-tribromobenzene). Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Bromine water cannot directly tribrominate nitrobenzene because the nitro group is strongly deactivating and meta-directing. Reduction to aniline is required before tribromination. Reductive deamination must follow diazotisation. Thus, the proper sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_SEQUENCING_Q08 - Multistep synthesis of fluorotoluene from nitrotoluene

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following synthetic transformations in the correct chronological sequence for the multistep conversion of 4-nitrotoluene to 4-fluorotoluene:

I. Reduction of 4-nitrotoluene with iron scrap and hydrochloric acid to yield 4-methylaniline.
II. Diazotisation of 4-methylaniline with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at 273–278 K to form 4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride.
III. Treatment of 4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride with fluoroboric acid to precipitate 4-methylbenzenediazonium fluoroborate.
IV. Thermal decomposition of dry 4-methylbenzenediazonium fluoroborate to isolate 4-fluorotoluene.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Chemical Transformations
Starting material: 4-nitrotoluene (\(\text{CH}_3-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{NO}_2\)). Target product: 4-fluorotoluene (\(\text{CH}_3-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{F}\)).

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Synthetic Strategy
Direct fluorination of toluene cannot be carried out due to explosive reactivity and cleavage of the alkyl side chain. Moreover, nucleophilic displacement of the nitro group in 4-nitrotoluene is not feasible. The classical synthetic route highlighted in NCERT involves reduction of the nitro group to an amine, conversion to a diazonium salt, and Balz–Schiemann fluorination.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Analysis
In Stage I, 4-nitrotoluene is reduced using iron scrap and hydrochloric acid (\(\text{Fe} / \text{HCl}\)) to produce 4-methylaniline (also called p-toluidine). In Stage II, 4-methylaniline is diazotised by treatment with nitrous acid (\(\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}\)) at 273–278 K, yielding 4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride. In Stage III, fluoroboric acid (\(\text{HBF}_4\)) is added to the cold diazonium solution, precipitating water-insoluble 4-methylbenzenediazonium fluoroborate (\(\text{CH}_3-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N}_2^+\text{BF}_4^-\)). In Stage IV, the dry diazonium fluoroborate salt is heated gently. It undergoes controlled thermal decomposition, evolving nitrogen and boron trifluoride gases while delivering 4-fluorotoluene.

Step 4: Chronological Sequence Assembly
The consecutive transformations proceed logically as: Stage I (reduction of nitro to primary amine) \(\rightarrow\) Stage II (diazotisation) \(\rightarrow\) Stage III (fluoroborate precipitation) \(\rightarrow\) Stage IV (thermal cleavage to 4-fluorotoluene). Hence, the correct chronological sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Diazotisation requires the primary aromatic amine intermediate, so reduction must be the first stage. Salt isolation must precede pyrolysis. Therefore, the unique valid sequence is \(\text{I} \rightarrow \text{II} \rightarrow \text{III} \rightarrow \text{IV}\).
